title: Night prayer
hook: the short prayer before sleep, with the Nunc Dimittis of Simeon
carry: now let your servant go in peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Liturgy of the Hours, the Church's clock of psalms. Your line was someone is always praying. Did you picture them, somewhere, at your sunset? Today, the last hour of that clock. Day two hundred forty-one.

Think about the last ten minutes of your day. For most of us it's a phone, face-lit in the dark, scrolling until the thing falls on our nose. The last thing we take in is usually the loudest thing we could find. For more than a thousand years, monks, nuns, priests and, more and more, ordinary Catholics have ended the day a different way. The lights go down. The house goes quiet. And they pray one short, gentle hour, the last of the day, before they sleep. It takes about ten minutes. It ends with an old man in the Temple holding a baby. Today's word is that last hour.
screen: `THE LAST TEN MINUTES OF THE DAY.` → `A SHORT, GENTLE HOUR.` → `AN OLD MAN HOLDING A BABY.`

segments.voice: Compline comes from the Latin completorium, the completing. It's the hour that finishes the day. First, the shape. It begins by looking back. In today's Liturgy of the Hours there's a short examination of conscience: what did today hold, what do I regret, what am I grateful for. Then a psalm or two, often Psalm 90 in the old numbering, the psalm about resting in the shadow of the Most High. Then a short reading, and a response taken from the psalms: into thy hands I commend my spirit. Jesus said that line on the cross. Here it's said before sleep, and the two are meant to echo. Second, the song. The heart of Compline is the canticle of Simeon, from Luke's Gospel. Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the Temple. An old man named Simeon had been promised he wouldn't die before he saw the Christ. He takes the baby in his arms and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; because my eyes have seen thy salvation." In Latin it begins Nunc dimittis, now you dismiss, and that's its name. Third, why at night. Simeon is ready to let go. He's seen what he waited for, and he can rest. The Church puts his words on our lips at the edge of sleep, a small daily practice of letting go. Fourth, the close. Compline ends with a hymn to Mary, often the Salve Regina, and then the house keeps silence until morning.
screen: `COMPLETORIUM: THE COMPLETING.` · `LOOK BACK, A PSALM, INTO THY HANDS.` · `SIMEON HOLDS THE CHILD.` · `A DAILY PRACTICE OF LETTING GO.` · then, large: `NOW THOU DOST DISMISS THY SERVANT, O LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end a day the way Compline does. Settle and breathe. Look back over today, quickly and kindly. One thing you regret. One thing you're grateful for. Then, if you pray, you can say Simeon's words slowly: Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace. If you don't pray, just picture the old man handing the baby back, and let your own day be handed back too. The bell holds the time.
Compline. From the Latin for completing: the last hour of the Church's day, prayed before sleep, with the song of Simeon at its heart. Today's word.
Your line: now let your servant go in peace. Tonight, give the last five minutes before sleep to quiet instead of a screen, and let the day be finished. Day two hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Monks and nuns pray Compline together before the night silence, and many Catholics pray it alone from a breviary or an app; it includes an examination of conscience, psalms, a short reading, the Nunc Dimittis and a closing antiphon to Mary.

fork.setup: you're Simeon. you were promised you'd see the Christ before you died, and now a young couple hands you their baby. what do you say?
options: ask God for more years to watch him grow.
say you can go now in peace, because you've seen it.
say nothing, and hand him back.
fork.reveal: "now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace." he's ready to let go, and the Church sings his words every night.

original.note: Latin: now you dismiss. the first words of Simeon's song in the Latin Bible, and its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old word for a bedtime prayer.
what it means: completorium, the completing. the last hour of the Church's day, ending with Simeon's song of letting go.
what a scholar hears: the Rule of Saint Benedict already sets Compline before the night silence; the hour is well over a thousand years old.
